articles.title_zh: Investors Who Piled Into China's AI Boom Just Watched About $480 Billion Vanish in Under Four Months. Are America's AI Bulls Next? - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
China's AI stocks just staged one of the most dramatic collapses in recent market history, and Wall Street is now asking whether the same warning signs that preceded the crash are quietly flashing across American portfolios.
Market Pulse desk. Editor: AJ Tiarsmith, PhD .
China’s hottest trade of 2026 has become its most painful. The STAR 50, Shanghai’s index of artificial intelligence and chip companies, has fallen 40% from its July high, according to Reuters reporting. Per the same report, the collapse erased about $480 billion in market value over roughly four months.
That figure is a paper decline across the whole index. Actual losses depended on when investors bought. Investors who bought before the summer run-up may still be ahead. Investors who bought in July and August took most of the damage.
Dong Baozhen, a Beijing-based fund manager, gave Reuters a blunt verdict: “The stock market later evolved into a speculative crazy bull. And now we see the bubble bursting.” Beijing appears to have seen trouble coming. Reuters re[prts state-backed investors sold into rallies during the run-up, a sign policymakers wanted to cool the boom.
The victims read like a list of China’s AI champions, per Trending Topics citing Reuters. Humanoid robot maker Unitree has lost about half its value since its August debut. GPU developers MetaX and Moore Threads, seen as China’s answer to NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ), have roughly halved since July. Optical module suppliers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink trade about 60% below their summer highs. Memory chip maker CXMT fell more than 25% in the month before Oct. 27.
The damage goes well beyond Shanghai’s tech board. Goldman Sachs ( NYSE:GS ) estimates that AI stocks account for 42% of China’s market value and 57% of its trading. When one theme carries that much weight, a reversal hits the whole country’s market.
Valuations help explain how fast the drop came. Trending Topics reported that the STAR 50’s price-to-earnings ratio once stood near 250 and still sits around 100 after the crash, compared with about 30 for the Nasdaq 100, without saying whether those are trailing or forward measures.
Americans felt this directly. The KraneShares China Technology & Semiconductor STAR 50 Index ETF ( NYSEARCA:KSTR ), the main way U.S. investors hold the index, fell 42.63% from the June 30 close through noon Oct. 28. It lost 21.02% in the past month alone and trades at $18.56. That leaves it 0.27% lower for the year, which means the entire summer rally is gone.
Over the same window, the Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ), a stand-in for the Nasdaq 100, slid 1.9% and is down 2.97% over the past month. It remains up 17.6% year to date. Both markets are riding the same AI theme, and the results could hardly be further apart.
Morgan Stanley ( NYSE:MS ) forecasts that offshore Chinese stocks will fall another 10% to 15% before bottoming, according to Yahoo Finance. If that forecast is right, the correction has further to go.
For U.S. investors, China’s selloff works better as a checklist than a forecast. Three warning signs came before the STAR 50’s drop: extreme valuations, heavy concentration in one theme and crowded trading. The U.S. shows softer versions of all three. NVIDIA alone was 7.6% of QQQ’s net assets at the end of June, and chip and AI hardware names fill much of the fund’s top holdings. A Nasdaq 100 multiple near 30 is high, though still far below the STAR 50’s peak.
The signal to track next quarter is whether QQQ’s top holdings take an even bigger share of the fund while hyperscaler spending plans hold steady. Rising concentration without rising earnings is the pattern Shanghai just punished. For KSTR holders, the past four months show how hard a single-country, single-theme fund can swing. A broad index spreads that risk across many sectors, while KSTR concentrates it in one. Riding an AI theme is reasonable as long as the exit plan is written down in advance, which is the entire subject of our free bubble survivor’s handbook .

articles.content_orig:
Taco-bout bearish. There are a lot of big earnings after today's close, including Microsoft, Google, T-Mobile and Ford. But it's one fast food giant that apparently has options traders most worried: Chipotle. Options trading exploded in Chipotle Tuesday on volume more than eight times its monthly average and skewed heavily towards puts, with 240,000 puts trading versus under 17,000 calls. Of the $8 million in put premiums, at least $2 million of it came from someone buying back 56,000 25-strike puts for Nov. 6 expiry that they had likely sold, while simultaneously selling the same number of 22.5-strike puts expiring mid-December, arguably on the margin an indication of weakening confidence as CMG's nears the trader's first strike and forces a roll down in price and out in time to give room for the stock to slip further. Separately, there was another outright bearish bet: around 11:30 a.m. E.T, someone bought 7,500 28-strike puts expiring Nov. 20, a $1.1 million bet that needs Chipotle to drop another 5% the next 3.5 weeks. "All of these look like earnings plays and our data show customers generally bearish," said Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner at Volland, options positioning platform.
The $27 level is an interesting one from a technical perspective. It the shoulder line of a large head and shoulders pattern that goes back to January of 2021. Technicians often view a break below a ridge line as bearish price action. "The last time Chipotle implied move before earnings was this low was July 2025 and the stock got crushed," DeLorenzo added.

articles.title_orig: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.title_zh: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.content_orig:
BARCELONA, Spain — At least 68 people were killed and 68 injured when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, sending carriages careering off the tracks, in the second major accident on the same line in less than a year.
“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail,” one passenger, Miguel, told Spain’s COPE radio, adding that he was traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains.
“Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train — I imagine it must have been the other one,” he added.
Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off.  Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo.
As rescue teams continued to search through the wreckage ‌of ​the ‌derailed ⁠carriages, the Castilla-La Mancha ‌regional government said ‌68 people had been killed and 68 injured. Together the two trains were carrying more than 500 passengers.
Several U.S. citizens were among the injured, according to a State Department spokesperson, who said the U.S. is continuing to work with local authorities to identify all Americans involved and provide them consular assistance.
“We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of all those affected,” the spokesperson said. “We encourage U.S. citizens in the area to notify loved ones of their safety and monitor local media for updates.”
At the site of the crash on Wednesday, Prime Minister of Spain Pedro Sánchez said: “The government of Spain and the whole state are with the victims and also with the families of the victims.”
Sánchez, who is facing a snap election next month, said the government was investigating the cause of the crash and any failures, vowing action “if there has been negligence.”
He said that the country must restore confidence in its high-speed rail network, with the crash coming after a separate disaster on the same rail line killed 46 people in January. “It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to have two high-speed accidents in less than a year,” he said.
Spain’s transport minister Oscar Puente said Wednesday’s crash ⁠occurred after a state-owned Renfe high-speed train was authorized ⁠to ​continue its ⁠journey despite an active red ⁠signal and ⁠a stationary ‌train from private rail company Iryo on the tracks ahead.
Addressing ‌reporters in ‌Madrid, Puente said ⁠the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure which automatically stopped ‌traffic. An erroneous ​decision was ‌made ⁠to restart the ⁠Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said.
Locals rushed to the scene of the accident, which has prompted a major national emergency response and raised questions about the safety and security of Spain’s high-speed rail infrastructure, which had previously been hailed as among the most sophisticated in Europe.
Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, told state broadcaster TVE that the trains were heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville when one ran into the tail of the other, which had stopped on the line.
She added that some 397 people had been traveling on the Renfe train and 147 people on the Iryo train.
Spain’s royal family who said they shared “in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Spanish political parties said Wednesday they would briefly pause campaigning ahead of next month’s general election. Spain’s football federation also said it would postpone some of its Copa del Rey soccer fixtures, following the collision.
Aerial footage shows aftermath of deadly crash
Juan Manuel Moreno, the president of the Andalusian regional government, said on X that there would be three days of mourning in the region.
The full scale of the disaster remains unclear but officials said an emergency phone line had been set up for families of the victims; local blood banks had also made appeals for donations.
Manuel Galan, the mayor of the nearby municipality of Urda, said he had been asked by emergency services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.
Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Spain’s Cadena SER radio that she felt a strong impact that threw her forward and she initially thought the train had made an emergency stop.
After climbing down an embankment to safety, she said she saw part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage. “I saw dead people,” she added.
Salvador Arriza, a 62-year-old employee of Airbus, was travelling to the rear of the Renfe train.
He told the Reuters news agency the carriage ended up “completely wrecked, with seats being ripped out.”
“I was lucky because I was in a backward-facing seat, and the impact pushed me into it,” he added. “After the first hit I was disoriented, but the worst thing was that the train then kept moving for quite some time from the inertia and that’s when I thought something would happen to me.”
Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said.
Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe for trains moving more than 155 mph, with more than 1,900 miles of track, according to the European Union.
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.
Daniella Silva is a national reporter for NBC News, focusing on immigration.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

Toledo, Spain 6:07 p.m. Oct. 28
A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another in Spain on Wednesday morning near the central city of Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said, in one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history.
The cause of the crash, which sent parts of both trains down a rural embankment, was not immediately clear. It was the second lethal crash this year involving the same two rail operators, and it was likely to deepen doubts about the security of Spain’s once-vaunted rail system.
In Spanish news reports, passengers described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The crash also came about a month ahead of national elections, and it had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s left-wing government.
Sixty-eight people were seriously injured in the crash, 15 of them critically, said Emiliano García-Page, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region.
Spain’s rail authority, the Adif, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company,” both covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville. Renfe is the national rail provider.
Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.
Trains from the same operators collided on a southern line in January, leaving 46 people dead.
Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said on Wednesday that initial reports indicated two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed. He said all traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia route had been suspended until further notice.
Mr. Sánchez visited the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon, saying that Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” He declared three days of official mourning.
The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media soon after the crash. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.” His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.
Another deadly crash: In January , a northbound Iryo train derailed, two of its cars falling onto the opposite track, and a southbound Renfe train slammed into the carriages seconds later. An official report on what caused that lethal accident has not been released, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
A detailed account: In a news conference, Spain’s transportation minister described the events that he said preceded the crash on Wednesday.
José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.
The U.S. State Department said in a statement that several U.S. citizens were among those injured in the crash. It did not provide information about their conditions.
Spain’s transportation minister said a train crash that killed dozens on Wednesday appeared to result from an “inexplicable” decision by traffic control operators to tell a high-speed train to continue its journey when another train was stopped farther along the tracks.
The minister, Óscar Puente, said he spent the morning watching a reconstruction of the accident and listening to audio recordings of communications between the control center in Madrid and the trains that crashed near Toledo, and he gave a detailed account of what he said preceded the crash at a news conference.
At about 8:30 a.m. local time, an automatic train control system near the site of the crash went down because of a computer failure, Mr. Puente said.
The system — known as the Linienzugbeeinflussung or LZB — dates to the 1960s and uses external technologies, such as track circuits and axel counters, to monitor the speed and position of trains. This information allows the system to automatically calculate when and how quickly a train can safely move forward. It then changes railroad signals accordingly.
On Wednesday, the safety system was inactive along a stretch of about 39 miles, or 63 kilometers, of tracks, so six trains traveling along that section were automatically stopped as a precaution. At that point, he said, the control center in Madrid took over.
“The control center communicated with the trains that had stopped, and at 8:36 a.m., the decision was made to allow the train that eventually collided with the stationary Iryo train to resume its journey as normal,” Mr. Puente said, referring to the private rail operator of the stopped train.
Traffic controllers working for Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s rail infrastructure, told the train that eventually rear-ended the other to restart its planned journey, Mr. Puente said, “despite there being another train ahead of it.”
The train that was hit from behind was believed to have received instructions from traffic operators to continue, he said, but for unknown reasons it did not proceed.
The moving train then hit the stationary train.
“And that is the origin of the accident that has taken place,” Mr. Puente said, adding that the moving train should have been stopped according to protocol.
The Madrid-Seville route is currently undergoing a modernization program that will replace the LZB system with the more modern European Rail Traffic Management System. Infrastructure officials hope that the new system will cut down on human error in signaling.
Mr. Puente also said that the driver of an uninvolved train tried to warn the control center of the dangers when its operators greenlit the rear train’s resumption of its journey. That driver told the control center operator that trains should proceed at lower-than-normal speeds. The operator, Mr. Puente said, acknowledged his error. “Oh, yes,” the operator replied.
K. R. Callaway contributed reporting.
When the crash happened, Yahadi Mohamed Maulud, 41, who lives in the nearby town of Yébenes, loaded his car with water bottles and rushed to help. “We found a massacre,” he said, describing torn limbs and a blood-covered woman searching for her brother. One of the first to arrive at the scene, he helped to move injured passengers and carry stretchers. Mr. Maulud said he often took the train himself to Madrid for business, but no more: “I’m never getting on that train again.”
So many people showed up at Madrid hospitals on Wednesday to donate blood for victims of the train crash that the authorities are asking citizens to wait until Thursday or the following days, when more donations will be needed.
“The response from the people of Madrid to the call for blood donations is overwhelming,” said Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid’s regional president. “Thank you, everyone.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon. “It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while today’s accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced.

articles.title_zh: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.content_orig:
Study suggests the long-term fate of the solar system, including Earth, ‘may be far more complicated than predicted’, according to scientist
When a star like our sun grows old, it puffs up into a red giant that can gobble up its nearest planets.
But Chinese astronomers say they have found three solar systems where planets should have been eaten this way yet somehow survived – a puzzle that could change how scientists picture Earth’s distant future.
Using Nasa’s TESS space telescope, a team led by Qian Shengbang from Yunnan University showed that three Jupiter-like planets – each hugging an ageing star in the northern sky – had lived through their hosts ballooning out past them before shrinking back.

articles.title_orig: Apple announces its first touchscreen MacBook Pro
articles.title_zh: Apple announces its first touchscreen MacBook Pro
articles.content_orig:
Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touch screen, which it is calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.
Apple said that the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles. It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said on Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current pro laptops.
It's still an Apple laptop, and is running MacOS, not a version of the iPhone or iPad operating system. In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images. It also has a glowing Apple logo on the laptop's lid.
The new laptop will go on sale on Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models.
This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases. It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature.
"Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles.
The new MacBook Pro comes at a time when the laptop market has been going through one of its worst slumps ever. Overall shipments are expected to be down 11% this year. Analysts say the AI-driven global market shortage of memory has contributed to higher laptop prices, which has hurt sales and demand.
In the third quarter, total PC shipments dropped 20% on a year-over-year basis, according to market researcher IDC. Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate.
Even Apple's not immune to rising memory prices, after former CEO Tim Cook warned this summer that the situation around memory prices was "unsustainable." Nearly all Macs got price hikes this year. Mac Minis introduced in August got a $300 bump, for example.
The announcement caps a busy two months of product launches under Ternus.
Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June. Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor.
In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions.
The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone. In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue.
But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps. And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud.
Meta's AI model developer team bought hundreds of Mac Minis this year to test agents, for example. And Apple notably teamed up with Meta earlier this month to make an announcement that large, nearly frontier models can run on clusters of Macs connected with high-speed cabling, allowing developers to run agentic code without paying Anthropic or OpenAI.
Apple has had a historical resistance to touchscreen laptops — software chief Craig Federighi explained in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. "We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad. It's totally optimized for that. And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven't really felt a reason to change that," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal's Joanna Stern in 2021.
Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's. Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement .
That may be why Ternus in his early days as CEO will be the executive to backtrack on a long-running Apple design philosophy.
Touchscreen laptops have been available on Windows machines for a long time, but they're just another feature, not a selling point behind most purchasing decisions, Ryan Reith, IDC VP for worldwide device trackers, said.
Only 17% of notebook PCs shipped globally this year will have touchscreens, according to IDC data. Touchscreen laptops also have a slightly lower average selling price than non-touchscreen notebooks.
Hardware technology hasn't been the limiting factor for Apple merging its desktop and mobile interfaces, he added, and Apple could have been waiting to launch a touchscreen laptop until it could present a good user experience and perfect its software after attempts to make its iPad more like a laptop.
"This is really a user interface and software thing," Reith said. "It's one more thing that can draw the developers in."

Amid reports Iran had rejected the latest proposal for peace from Qatari intermediaries, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that his country was reviewing ideas for a diplomatic solution to the eight-month war.
"While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi wrote. "We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."
The seven-day plan was presented to the U.S. shortly after the U.N. General Assembly in September. However, President Trump rejected the idea presented by Iran for a seven-day ceasefire and then phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
A source had earlier reported there were concerns Israel could begin a new bombing campaign after its election, according to Reuters.
Kuwait summoned Iran's envoy in protest on Wednesday, after Tehran denied one of its citizens, sentenced to death in Kuwait, was involved in an assassination plot targeting a top government figure.
Earlier this week, two Kuwaiti judicial sources told the AFP news agency that the Gulf state had condemned three Shia men to death for plotting the assassination of Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Fahad al-Yousef, collaborating with Iran; and for membership in Hezbollah.
Iran's embassy in Kuwait said earlier Wednesday it "rejects the Kuwaiti government's claim regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate figures or in any other act that could harm Kuwaiti national security."
It added that the person in question had been outside Kuwait for 10 years.
It said it regretted a "negative approach towards Iran, manifested, among other things, in the repetition of flimsy and worn-out scenarios concerning Iranian interference in Kuwaiti affairs."
In response, Kuwait summoned Iranian ambassador Mohammad Toutounji over the statement, which it said "constituted blatant interference in the internal affairs of the State of Kuwait and an infringement upon its sovereignty and the independence of its judiciary."
Abdulredha Haydar Dahqani was among those who had been sentenced to death, the judicial sources told AFP.
Dahqani, an Iranian national, had already been handed the death penalty in 2016 after he was tried in absentia along with 25 Kuwaitis. He was convicted of spying for Iran and plotting attacks.
Another was Hussein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Kuwait's most influential Shia movement, the sources said.
Israel's defense minister on Wednesday denounced opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot for urging the military to resist post-election pressure from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has threatened new strikes on Iran.
"His call to senior military officials not to obey the directives of the prime minister or me or of other relevant security authorities, on the grounds that 'they have his support,' is an anti-democratic statement detached from reality," Israel Katz wrote on X .
Eisenkot, a former military chief, said in a speech to supporters after Tuesday's election that Netanyahu was a caretaker prime minister lacking a mandate and the military should serve the state rather than the premier.
"Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you. You have my unequivocal backing. Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened in recent days to renew strikes on Iran.
Media reports, denied by Netanyahu, said military chief Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir pushed back immediately before the election on the prime minister's new plans on Iran.
Eisenkot's comments were the latest in "a campaign of lies" about tension between Netanyahu and the military over Iran, Katz said.
Yemen's Ministry of Transport has warned of risks to civil aviation safety after Aden International Airport was targeted in a missile attack attributed to the Houthi group for the sixth time, Saudi Arabia's Asharq News reported.
The missile strike shook parts of the southern city, raising fresh concerns over the safety of airport operations and the potential threat to civilian air traffic.

articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve 's interest rate decision Wednesday likely will be short on suspense, with markets expecting the central bank to stay on hold even with inflation tracking well above target.
Markets are pricing in less than a 10% chance that the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee follows up its quarter-percentage-point hike in September with another increase, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Assuming that sentiment is correct, it will leave the Fed's benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75% and 4% — and shift investor attention to Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and whatever clues he chooses to provide in his post-meeting news conference.
Traders expect the Fed to follow up the October skip with a hike at its next meeting in December.
While the Federal Reserve is largely expected to stand pat on its key interest rate on Wednesday, consumer rates have edged higher since policymakers pushed through their first hike last month.
The average 30-year fixed rate mortgage now sits at 7.33%, up from 7.12% last month, according to MND. Mortgage rates are closely tied to movement in the 10-year Treasury yield, which is now just below 5%.
The cost of borrowing against the equity in your dwelling – a home equity loan – has also risen and is now at 8.77%, versus 8.28% in September, according to Bankrate.
Savers have seen some marginal gains in the past month since the Fed lifted its rate by a quarter percentage point in September. The average money market annual yield is now at 0.45%, up one basis point from last month, according to Haver. The annual percentage yield on a five-year certificate of deposit is at 1.83%, up eight basis points from September, per Haver.
— Darla Mercado, Nick Wells
Fed funds futures traders now widely expect the central bank to keep rates unchanged today. But that wasn't always the case.
Futures indicate a nearly 93% likelihood that rates are holding steady, according to the latest data from CME's FedWatch tool. A month earlier, traders were forecasting a less than 30% probability of rates staying unchanged.
The market adjusted expectations as Fed officials signaled that the central bank can take its time before making another move. New York Fed President John Williams said "there is no need for urgency" after its September hike, which was the central bank's first in three years. Philip Jefferson, the Fed's vice chair, said members of the central bank would "need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time." Jefferson noted that yields increased following the Fed's September decision, indicating that investors are watching macroeconomic shifts.
The Federal Reserve's decision to raise rates at its last meeting boosted borrowing costs, and the expectation that more rate increases are in the pipeline means consumers are unlikely to see much relief anytime soon. Those elevated borrowing costs are adding to existing affordability challenges, particularly for lower- and middle-income consumers.
As long as the Federal Reserve keeps rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, consumers are unlikely to see much relief. Elevated borrowing costs are adding to existing affordability challenges, particularly for lower- and middle-income consumers.
Higher rates continue to affect credit cards, auto loans and mortgages. Credit card rates have climbed to their highest levels since late 2025, while 30-year mortgage rates have remained above 7%, making homeownership less affordable. Auto loan rates have also stayed near 7%, with even higher rates common in the used-car market.
One bright spot is savings. High-yield savings accounts continue to offer relatively strong returns compared with traditional bank accounts.
Some experts suggest consumers can ease budget pressures by paying down high-interest debt, negotiating better loan terms and taking advantage of higher yields on savings.
The Fed's big problem today is explaining why it's holding rates steady when the inflation rate has worsened since its last meeting – and several indicators suggest more bad numbers to come.
Start with tomorrow's PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation indicator. Both Wall Street and the Fed are able to use the CPI and PPI to pretty much peg the change in the PCE. The headline is expected to rise 0.5% for September , which will boost the year-over-year rate to 3.7% from 3.4%. The Fed could look past that, assuming it's driven by the continued rise in energy prices. But the core rate is seen rising 0.3%, raising the annual rate by a tenth to 3.1%.
What about the much-touted three-month annualized rate, which many doves have promoted as showing that inflation is under control? It fell to 2.05% last month, almost spot on with the Fed's 2% target. Time to cut, right? Not so fast. Model in a 0.3% rise in the core and the 3-month annualized rate shoots up to 2.7%. The Cleveland Fed's inflation nowcasting gauge sees core PCE in October running at 0.25%. Model that number in and the three-month annualized rate would rise to 3.24% in October. The takeaway: the gauge is so volatile that it serves as a poor guide for monetary policy.
The Cleveland Fed's trimmed mean, which removes extreme price changes from the CPI, has hovered between 2.6% and 2.7% for most of this year, showing little change. The Dallas Fed's trimmed mean has stood mostly alone in supporting a dovish take on inflation at 2.2%. It's worth noting, however, the Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan has herself cautioned that the measure may do too extreme a job of trimming away inflation.
Another problem the Fed faces: a seasonal pattern of inflation spiking up at the beginning of the year. Goldman Sachs sees inflation easing next year as pressures from tariffs, the AI buildout and energy abate. But it worries, "companies could take the opportunity provided by start-of-the-year price increases to pass along their higher costs, resulting in a larger 'January effect.' "
The danger of a hold today amid current inflationary pressures is that the Fed may need to do more in coming months. TD Securities writes: "It only takes one notably bad inflation report and/or a collection of strong labor market data for the market to start pricing larger odds of a 50bp rate increase in upcoming meetings."
Markets were taking a cautious approach ahead of the Fed rate decision, with major indexes mostly positive and Treasury yields also higher.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average is up less than 100 points, while the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were around the flatine.
In the fixed income market, the benchmark 10-year note added about 3.6 basis points to yield 5.03%, while the 2-year note added 3.7 basis points to 4.774%.
Since Kevin Warsh took over as Fed chairman in May, stocks have generally fallen on Fed meeting days, then posted gains the day after, according to DataTrek Research cofounder Nicholas Colas. The S&P 500 in particular has rallied at least 1% on the three post-meeting days of Warsh's tenure.
The Fed's decision Wednesday follows a string of reports indicating that inflation is reaccelerating.
September's consumer price index showed annual inflation ticked up to 3.7%, driven by higher energy costs. The CPI is currently on one of its longest streaks of annual readings above 2% on record.
The producer price index rose to 6.3% year over year in September. It was the steepest 12-month increase since 2022 for the index, which acts as a gauge of inflation on wholesalers.
The Fed won't get the latest from its preferred inflation reading, the personal consumption expenditures price index, until the September number is released Thursday morning. Wall Street economists use CPI and PPI use to estimate PCE, and they expect it to rise as well.

Jerusalem 6:42 p.m. Oct. 28
Isabel Kershner Johnatan Reiss Aaron Boxerman Qasim Nauman and Leo Sands
Israel’s political leaders were poised for weeks of negotiations over the shape of the next government, as initial results on Wednesday showed no clear winner in a tightly fought election that many have described as a make-or-break moment for the country.
If neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-line alliance nor an opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot win enough seats to form a government, both would need to find support from outside their blocs for backing as prime minister.
By Wednesday afternoon, election officials had counted more than 70 percent of ballots. Those votes, alongside exit polls, indicate that neither bloc would reach the 61 seats needed to secure a straightforward majority in the Knesset, Israel’s Parliament.
Some of Mr. Netanyahu’s allies are floating the idea that he could join Mr. Eisenkot and other centrists to form a broad unity government to stay in power. For Mr. Netanyahu, the long-serving prime minister who remains as a caretaker until a government is formed, that would be a comfortable scenario, as long as he remained on top.
His primary rival, Mr. Eisenkot, faces a dilemma of his own: He has denounced Mr. Netanyahu as unfit to lead Israel, but he has also objected to partnering with Arab parties in a potential coalition. The two Arab parties are projected to win as many as 17 seats — a remarkable show of strength that could make them Mr. Eisenkot’s only path to toppling Mr. Netanyahu.
On Wednesday, Mr. Eisenkot did not explicitly mention the Arab parties and instead pledged to build “a stable Zionist government.”
Most of the votes were expected to be counted by Wednesday, though the final tally could take days. Lengthy negotiations could follow as political parties try to assemble a governing majority. If those talks fail, the country could head to a second round of elections — a scenario that has played out before. For Mr. Netanyahu, running down the clock in the hope of securing a stronger showing in a fresh election could be his strongest shot at retaining his role as prime minister.
The uncertainty did not stop the leading candidates from making triumphant late-night speeches to their supporters.
Mr. Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, struck a defiant tone toward Mr. Netanyahu, saying: “Tonight we got the answer: The public opted for change.”
A few hours later, Mr. Netanyahu told supporters that his party, Likud, had emerged as the largest in Israel. “We must form a strong right-wing government,” he said.
Here’s what else we are covering:
Herzog’s role: President Isaac Herzog of Israel holds a largely ceremonial position, except after national elections, when it falls to him to select a potential prime minister. Read more ›
More votes: The exit polls do not reflect the hundreds of thousands of votes cast at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In Israel’s 2022 election, those votes tended to favor Mr. Netanyahu and his allies.
Regional implications: Israel’s neighbors in the Middle East had little hope that the election would fundamentally change Israel’s security doctrine, which has hardened since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023. Read more ›
Initial results: The 70 percent of the votes counted indicate that Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition will receive about 54 seats, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc will get roughly 49, and the Arab parties will reach 17. But the numbers could still easily shift.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is persisting with unproven allegations that Israel’s Arab voters have “stolen the elections.” Israel’s official elections committee has said there was no indication of widespread irregularities in the election on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the Likud again said that Arab parties — which are expected to receive a historically high number of parliamentary seats — had stolen the vote and called for the police and intelligence services to investigate.
Analysts say that Netanyahu is trying to de-legitimize votes by Arab citizens of Israel, fearing that his leading Jewish Israeli opponents might try to link up with the newly empowered Arab political bloc in an effort to unseat him.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel fell short of outright victory on Tuesday night. But he has still emerged with a good chance of clinging to power.
Mr. Netanyahu, 77, has plenty of political blessings to count after the vote. His Likud party is set to remain the largest in the Israeli Parliament, defying the pre-election polls. His rivals, led by the former general Gadi Eisenkot, secured far less support and have been left more divided than expected.
Analysts say the result, with neither bloc securing enough votes to form a clear majority, could easily lead to weeks or months of political gridlock — a scenario that suits Mr. Netanyahu just fine. He will remain in charge as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed or new elections have to be held.
It is a remarkable turnaround for Mr. Netanyahu, whose critics blamed him for failing to prevent the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day in Israeli history. A consummate political survivor of more than three decades in Israeli politics, Mr. Netanyahu is famous for out-negotiating and manipulating almost every opponent who has tried to end his rule.
“Netanyahu is still in the driver’s seat,” said Natan Sachs, an expert on Israeli politics at the Middle East Institute, a Washington-based research group. “He’s still in control of most events, and that’s where he likes to be.”
Mr. Netanyahu, the longest serving prime minister in Israeli history, still has some headaches. The hard-line coalition he formed in 2022 — the most far-right in Israeli history — is set to lose its majority in Israel’s 120-member Parliament.
Mr. Netanyahu could also end up losing if Mr. Eisenkot, whose bloc trails the prime minister’s coalition by several seats, chooses to work with the Arab parties that performed better than ever to oust him.
But Mr. Eisenkot is likely to struggle to form such an alliance, given how Israeli public opinion has shifted since the Oct. 7 attacks. Even though Arab leaders in Israel generally condemned the attacks, many Jewish Israelis still regard partnering with them as unacceptable.
“Netanyahu knew he was going to have a weaker bloc. But he knew that his goal, even if he couldn’t get a 61-seat majority, would be to prevent his rivals from forming a government,” said Mazal Mualem, who has written a biography of Mr. Netanyahu. “And it seems he’s succeeded.”
All this was hard to imagine just three years ago. Mr. Netanyahu’s public standing plunged after the Oct. 7 attacks, when 1,200 in Israel were killed and 250 were taken hostage, igniting the war in Gaza. Even fervent supporters of the prime minister feared his time in office would end because of his failure to prevent the catastrophe.
Mr. Netanyahu, however, has tenaciously clambered his way back without accepting any responsibility for the devastating security lapse. Instead, he blamed the assault on Israeli security chiefs, launched a series of military campaigns in Lebanon and Iran that killed some of Israel’s most significant foes, and ran his electoral campaign focused on amplifying fears of Israel’s Arab parties.
On Tuesday, a swath of Jewish Israelis threw their support behind him, defying Mr. Netanyahu’s critics at home and abroad. articles.title_zh: ‘Noah’s Ark remains’ found burned and buried 30 feet below final resting place: report
articles.content_orig:
They’re the real raiders of the lost Ark.
Researchers claim they’ve potentially discovered wood from Noah’s Ark in Eastern Turkey, potentially cracking a caper that has eluded believers for thousands of years.
The so-called discovery was reportedly made in the Durupınar Formation , a roughly 538-foot-long geological structure near Mount Ararat.
Discovered in 1959, site has fascinated Ark hunters for decades due to its ship shape and proximity to the events in the Bible.
In the religious text, the legendary vessel sheltered Noah, his family and Earth’s animals during an apocalyptic flood some 4,300 years ago.
After studying the repository for years, researchers feel they’ve found evidence that the site is indeed the Ark’s final resting place, dispelling theories that it formed naturally.
Andrew Jones, project head and founder of Noah’s Ark Scans, told the Daily Mail that they’ve discovered both charred and uncharred wood nearly 30 feet underground, which could potentially be “the charred remains of Noah’s Ark.”
However, Jones notes that the wood could entail the remains of a campfire a shepherd had started while sheltering inside the Ark hundreds of years ago.
Although they’re unsure if it was purposefully set alight or ignited via lightning strike or volcanic eruption.
Coincidentally, in the Bible story, Noah is told to cover the Ark in pitch, a waterproofing chemical that is also highly flammable.
According to the researchers, the blaze might’ve helped preserve the remnants by slowing the decomposition of wood in soil.
Either way, this marks the latest in a series of clues that supposedly support the boat’s biblical provenance.
Previously, Noah’s Ark Scans used ground-penetrating radar to map what they claim is a series of subterranean chambers and tunnels at the site, whose dimensions mirror those described in the bible.
These underground corridors reportedly led to a central cavity that Jones dubbed the “Atrium.”
“God told Noah to bring the animals in,” Jones told GB News in the Spring while explaining the alleged significance of the so-called quarters. “And so these animals would have stayed there, plus Noah and his family.”
Meanwhile, soil analysis revealed that the inside dirt harbored three times more organic matter  — and 38% more potassium — than samples taken right outside, hinting at its unnatural origins.
Jones said his team’s case was strengthened this past fall when a drilling and scanning expedition revealed that there was no natural bedrock beneath the formation as many critics claim.
Instead, they found rich black soil, which researchers plan to test for signs of decayed wood and other alleged signs of the Ark this winter.
“Noah’s Ark was a giant wooden boat, according to the Bible,” said Jones. “As wood decays, you’re gonna find elevated organic matter.”

articles.content_orig:
A woman said she locked herself in a bathroom after realising her then-husband had allowed someone else in the bedroom while she was blindfolded and having sex, a jury has heard.
In a police interview played at Winchester Crown Court, Joanne Young said she was restrained when she felt a hand on her wrist which she believed did not belong to her now ex-husband Philip Young.
Joanne - who has waived her legal right to anonymity - said Young, who has admitted drugging and raping her, later apologised and told her he had invited someone to watch the couple have sex after browsing online forums.
Four men who Young is alleged to have recruited to abuse his wife at their home are now on trial.
Warning: This story contains distressing details
On the second day of the four men's trial, two police interviews with Joanne were played to the court.
During the first interview, dated 29 July 2024, Joanne said the incident when she hid in the bathroom had happened in February 2023 after a night out with friends.
She told police she could not "remember all of it", but said Young had come upstairs after she had gone to bed.
Joanne said she "woke up with a blindfold and restraints on" and loosened the restraint on her right hand and then the left. At that point, she said, she felt a hand grip her wrist.
She said Young - who she believed was at the end of the bed - said "get down" to someone as she tried to take her blindfold off.
Joanne said she then saw someone ducking at the end of the bed and she ran to the bathroom and locked the door.
"The bed is a really big bed. So to have someone on the end of the bed and the left was not possible… I knew immediately," she told police.
The jury heard the couple discussed the incident, with Joanne telling police it was the first time she had ever seen her then-husband cry.
Joanne said she asked Young if he had ever invited anyone to watch them have sex before, which he denied.
"It was so intrusive. I was so upset. He knows I would have never said yes to that," she told police.
Joanne told the officer: "I didn't know if I should stay in the relationship or get myself out of the situation."
She said she took the incident as a "one-off" and tried to "move on".
Asked by an officer if there was a discussion between Young and Joanne about having someone else in the relationship, she said: "There was a joke years ago, a bit of banter, where he said in the kitchen something like 'would you ever want to sleep with someone else?'.
"I said no, and he said 'as long as I can watch you'. We laughed it off but it was a no."
She added: "It was never a part of our relationship. There'd never been a discussion. He never asked me what I wanted, it wasn't a conversation."
On the day Young was arrested, Joanne said he admitted to her he had shared images of her online without her consent.
Joanne said it had felt like a "kick in the stomach" and she was left in "shock and utter confusion".
She said: "How he could do that to me. How he could do something that's so intimate that's not allowed. How can he do it? How can you do that and think that was OK?"
The prosecution also read out statements from people who had been friends with Joanne and Young during their marriage.
Joanne's friend Susan said she thought the couple had a "dream relationship" before Joanne told her about the alleged incident of February 2023.
"She was in a real dark place about what happened," the statement said.
"After telling me, life went back to normal but what I witnessed from Jo was she didn't seem herself and that Phil had crossed a line from what he had done.
"Jo explained she was torn about why would Phil do this to her. She was in shock and seemed to be numb."
Emma Brown, who the court was told had been best friends with the couple since 2009, said Young "could handle his drink" and she "never saw him noticeably drunk".
"He was always on his mobile phone... I didn't know what he was doing as I didn't look at it," she added.
The four men jointly charged with Young, 50, are accused of the following offences:
Jurors were shown videos earlier which allegedly showed Sanderson-Doyle, Wilkins and Macksoni sexually assaulting Joanne.
Young, a former Conservative Swindon councillor, previously admitted 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing an obscene article.
He also published more than 500 intimate images and videos of his ex-wife and recorded her doing private acts for his own sexual gratification without her consent between 2010 and 2024.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
Young and Hamilton will be sentenced at the end of the trial, which is expected to last up to four weeks.

articles.content_orig:
The Department of Health and Human Services is giving compounding pharmacies a temporary green light to make six peptides while the agency continues to work on a formal rule change.
In a notice filed Wednesday, the agency said it would exercise “enforcement discretion,” meaning it will not take legal action against compounding pharmacies that make the six unapproved peptides. In practice, that means these pharmacies can start offering them now, even though the peptides aren’t yet on the Food and Drug Administration’s list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make.
The six peptides are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500.
They’ve been promoted online as treatments for everything from faster healing to younger-looking skin and a longer lifespan. None are approved by the FDA, and the agency’s own scientists concluded there is insufficient data to prove they are safe and effective.
The FDA said compounding pharmacies must certify the identity and purity of the compounds. They must also now report side effects, which was not previously mandated.
The move comes as a growing “gray market” has sprung up around peptides, where retailers sell them labeled “for research use only,” a legal workaround that lets them claim they aren’t meant for humans. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others have argued that allowing peptides to be compounded would move people away from this gray market and toward safer products.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, HHS is working to put prevention and patient safety at the center of health care—and that includes confronting the risks of black-market peptides,” Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said in a statement.
Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now leads the Center for Science in the Public Interest watchdog group, said the FDA was essentially “turning a blind eye” to widen access to drugs that have not been proven to work.
Compounding pharmacies generally may use only ingredients the FDA has added to an official list known as the bulk drugs substances list. Adding an ingredient requires the FDA to propose a rule, take public comment and issue a final rule, a process that can take several months.
The agency took a step toward that process in July, when an FDA advisory panel narrowly voted in favor of adding six peptides to the bulk list. The panel included six new appointees with ties to the peptide industry and another who is the son of a U.S. representative who has pushed Kennedy to make peptides more available. (During that meeting, some committee members expressed concerns that the recommendation could make it harder for the FDA to say no to other unapproved drugs in the future.)
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the FDA was scheduled to meet outside groups, including Medivant Healthcare, a compounding pharmacy that offers peptides, according to Reginfo.gov , a federal website that tracks government regulations.
Shabbir Safdar, executive director of the Partnership for Safe Medicines, which researches the dangers of counterfeit medicines, said both the enforcement discretion and upcoming rule change would expose Americans to “untested dangerous substances.”
“Imagine what it means for the nation’s top drug regulator to announce they won’t enforce the laws on people making completely untested compounds and distributing them to the public,” Safdar said.
Berkeley Lovelace Jr. is a health and medical reporter for NBC News. He covers the Food and Drug Administration, with a special focus on Covid vaccines, prescription drug pricing and health care. He previously covered the biotech and pharmaceutical industry with CNBC.

US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_orig: Confessions Of An SR-71 Blackbird Pilot
articles.title_zh: Confessions Of An SR-71 Blackbird Pilot
articles.content_orig:
Few humans have flown a jet as high or as fast as Adelbert “Buz” Carpenter. During his six years as an SR-71 Blackbird pilot, the now-retired Air Force colonel flew 230 missions, frequently exceeding three times the speed of sound. Over the course of nearly 800 hours flying one of the world’s most iconic aircraft, Carpenter soared over Cuba, skirted North Korea and tracked Russian nuclear submarines in the Arctic. He also had a few close calls, in one case narrowly avoiding disaster.
With the possibility that NASA could be returning the SR-71 to its test fleet, the Blackbird is back in the news and we wanted to dive deep into what it was like to fly the jet and get some thoughts on the latest SR-71 rumors from someone who piloted it. We couldn’t think of anyone better than “Buz” Carpenter.
Before joining the Blackbird program, Carpenter flew recon missions during the Vietnam War as an RF-4C pilot among other assignments. He now serves as a docent at the Smithsonian Air & Space Museum’s Udvar Hazy Center .
Some of the questions and answers have been lightly edited for clarity.
Q: How did you become an SR-71 pilot? Walk me through your decision to join the program. What made you want to fly it? What was the qualification process like?
A: Well, it was a multi-step process… You had to fill out all this paperwork. You had to send them your flight records, all your flight checks, your physical records. What are your professional ratings in the Air Force? Do they rate you as superior?
The home base was Beale Air Force Base in California. If they liked you, you got called back for about a week. The first two days were a modified astronaut’s physical. I mean, they checked everything. You had a series of interviews. As a pilot, I had to fly with two current SR-71 pilots, not in the SR, but in the companion trainer, the T-38 .
At any time, there were only 11 of us qualified to fly the SR-71. That’s how small a group it was for the whole program. Only 85 of us ever flew operational missions… So you can see it’s a pretty small group.
Q: Did pilots have to be invited to apply for the SR-71 program?
A: Oh, you had to apply for it. When there was a pilot in the program and he knew somebody he used to fly with that was really super, the invitation would be: ‘fill out the paperwork, and once we get the paperwork and look you over, we’ll call you back’ and go through the same routine that I went through.
You’ve got to go through the physical. Sometimes it was shortened because they knew the person. A couple of them were actually T-38 instructors at Beale Air Force Base, and their invitation was a lot shorter because they had all the records there. They knew who you were, and they knew how you could fly.
About a week before Christmas, 1974, I got a telegram that says ‘you’ve been selected. You will report to Beale Air Force Base July 1975 and commence training in the SR-71.’ I couldn’t have been happier.
Q: What was the training like?
A: The first thing you’re going to do is you’re going to get checked out in the T-38, even though we had all flown it earlier. You had to become [requalified] in it, because as long as you’re in a program, you’re going to continue to fly the T-38.
Once you actually started the program, you’d be paired with your navigator, who then assumed the title Reconnaissance Systems Officer [RSO]. And in my case, it was the wonderful Capt. John Murphy. We trained and flew together for four years.
Your first month or so was mostly academics, because the airplane was so different. You had to learn the systems because the airplane operates in a very hot environment — an average temperature of almost 600 degrees [Fahrenheit]. The airplane grows three to four inches in length, an inch or two in width — it’s 93% titanium to deal with the high temperatures [associated with supersonic flight]. So during flights, you are going to have to deal with systems that are now straining or starting to fail because of the heat environment they’re operating in. So it is imperative that you understand exactly how this airplane is engineered, and what kind of options you might have if you start getting failures.
Then you start getting into the simulator , and obviously it’s a kind of crawl-walk-run type of a deal. This was the first simulator I’d ever seen that was a computer simulator. Up until that point, they called them part-task trainers. It had all the switches and everything, but it didn’t fly like the airplane. Like you’d be in the trainer and they want to simulate a fire. Somebody would bang against the side of this thing, and yell ‘fire’ and turn on the fire light, but they were just watching what you were doing. The SR simulator flew exactly like you [would fly the plane].
So even before John and I started training, we would find times when the simulator wasn’t being used at night, and we would go down there, and fly this simulator. And if you did something wrong, it reacted exactly how the airplane would react. I mean, it could crash if you did something bad enough.
There’s no visual. The simulator could move a little bit motion-wise, not severely. It would react exactly how the airplane was going to react, but you couldn’t see anything. Your first visual of what the airplane was like was going to be on your first flight in the airplane.
That’s when you’re going to see what does a takeoff look like in 20 seconds? What does it look like to get behind a tanker and refuel? And as importantly, what does it look like to come back in at 175 indicated [airspeed] and land this airplane on a runway? It was a tremendous training aid because when you came back later on when you were doing your six weeks in Japan, maybe you took some vacation, but the first thing after that they’re going to put you in the simulator for four hours and see how you react to emergencies. It was very complex and defining. We washed people out who could not maintain the level of proficiency that we expected if you were going to fly this airplane.
Q: Could you practice refueling as well?
A: You could do takeoffs, because it was like an instrument takeoff, and you could do ‘quote’ instrument landings, but you had no visual to see how this whole thing would come together. Air refueling we didn’t mess with it because there wasn’t enough you could see. When you came to an air refueling in the simulator, they would just fill you up and say, ‘okay, you’ve been refueled.’ Because you needed the visual picture to understand what you’d be doing behind the tanker.
Q: Tell me about the first time you donned the pressure suit, which you had to wear to withstand the pressures of flying at altitudes of up to 80,000 feet or more.
A: If you were going to fly, you came in two and a half hours early. You had to pass a physical before every flight to make sure your sinuses and blood pressure and a number of other things were okay. You would then have a meal of steak and eggs, just like the astronauts, high protein, low bulk. They would brief you on the status of your airplane, and then about an hour and 15 minutes prior, you would go down where your suits were being maintained, and you’d put on cotton long johns because you’re going to perspire a little bit. Not profusely, but occasionally, if you were low on fuel. The fuel was the cooling system for the airplane, and if you’d been flying at the higher speeds, and you were low on fuel, the suit would heat up a little bit.
They’d suit you up. I’m going to stop there. The first time you ever suited up, you’re not going to the airplane. They’re just exposing you. It was a [NASA] Gemini suit that had been modified, and you put on the cotton long johns. You had two people that helped you into the suit. The suit is lying on the floor like a coverall. articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia has received 12 Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and announced a deal involving four S-400 air defence system batteries, strengthening its military capabilities as renewed fighting in the country raises security concerns.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the aircraft delivery during a visit to Moscow, where he attended a Russia-Africa summit and met Russian President Vladimir Putin .
“I would like to express my gratitude to my friend, Russian President Vladimir Putin, for his dedication in ensuring we received these warplanes a year ahead of our agreed schedule,” he said on his X account.
The Ethiopian leader did not disclose the value of the arms agreement, when the S-400 air defence systems would be delivered or where the aircraft and batteries would be deployed.
The acquisition comes as Ethiopia faces mounting security challenges, particularly in the northern Tigray region. A rebel alliance launched an offensive last month, raising fears of a renewed conflict following the war between 2020 and 2022 that killed hundreds of thousands of people.
During the previous conflict, Ethiopia relied heavily on foreign-made drones to strengthen its air power and turn the tide of fighting.
The latest escalation has also deepened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, which Addis Ababa accuses of supporting the rebels. Asmara has denied the allegations.
Ethiopia’s reported acquisition highlights Russia ’s continued efforts to deepen defence partnerships across Africa, where several countries rely on Russian aircraft and military equipment.
Sudan ’s Defence Ministry is reportedly negotiating with Moscow to acquire Su-30 and Su-35 fighter jets in exchange for allowing Russia to establish a major naval facility on the Red Sea, according to Military Watch Magazine.
Algeria , meanwhile, received a batch of Russian Su-34M strike fighters in May, adding to its substantial fleet of Russian-made military aircraft.
Earlier reports from Algerian defence publications indicated that the country had ordered 14 Su-34ME strike fighters, 14 Su-35E fighter jets and 14 Su-57E fifth-generation aircraft.
These deals underscore Russia’s continuing role in Africa’s defence procurement market, even as Moscow faces pressure on its military production and export capacity amid the war in Ukraine.

articles.title_zh: Bank of Canada raises key interest rate, says another hike possible
articles.content_orig:
Why now? Tiff Macklem asked what central bank aims to accomplish with rate hike
Bank of Canada's housing outlook 'pretty subdued' — but not just because of rates, official says
Canada's economy still resilient, but U.S. trade war taking its toll
How a potential interest rate hike could further slow the B.C. real estate market
We're wrapping up our live coverage of the Bank of Canada's interest rate announcement.
Here are some of the key takeaways from today's decision.
The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, marking its first change after seven consecutive holds and its first increase since July 2023.
Governor Tiff Macklem said the hike was "needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalized inflation."
As the war in the Middle East has kept oil prices high, the bank expects inflation to reach roughly 3.5 per cent by the end of 2026 and remain at or above three per cent for much of next year.
The bank's outlook for economic growth has improved slightly, though, with the Canadian economy expected to grow two per cent next year.
He also said the Canadian economy showed signs of resilience through the middle of 2026, growing 3.3 per cent in the second quarter.
Still, Macklem noted that uncertainty surrounding U.S. tariffs and the conflict in the Middle East continues to weigh on the economy.
Today's hike also means higher borrowing costs for Canadians, including prospective homebuyers.
Deputy governor Carolyn Rogers said the housing market is already struggling, particularly in Ontario and British Columbia, and that the rate increase will add to those pressures.
The bank hasn't ruled out more hikes, but Macklem stressed that future decisions will be made "one meeting at a time."
"There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully," the bank said.
Mortgage broker Marcus Tzaferis says today's rate decision might not do much to weigh on the housing market by keeping new buyers on the sidelines, because so many Canadians are already choosing not to buy.
But it will weigh on mortgage holders.
Those with variable rates will feel it the most. On a $500,000 mortgage, a rate hike of 25 basis points would add about $70 per month on average to a holder's monthly payments.
While that might not seem like much, Tzaferis says Canadians are already struggling with the high cost of living, pointing to a rise in insolvencies as a sign consumers are having a tough time.
"To a consumer that's already stretched, these 25 basis point incremental increases are going to have an impact," Tzaferis said.
For variable rate holders who are thinking about the impact that rising rates could have and want more predictability, Tzaferis says "now is the time" to try and lock in a fixed mortgage.
And for those who will need to renegotiate a mortgage within the next year, Tzaferis says they have the option to lock in a fixed rate further in advance, "almost like an insurance policy for themselves," which could make sense for some.
Pedro Antunes, chief economist at independent research firm Signal 49, says he thinks the bank could have held off longer before raising rates.
Looking at last month's inflation numbers, Antunes says inflation from oil still hasn't started spilling over into the cost of other prices yet. While the overall 3.1 inflation rate was high, core measures that strip out volatile items like oil were much lower and within the bank's target range.
"We haven't seen … a broader-based increase in prices, but I think that the bank has started to be concerned about what's coming down the road," Antunes told CBC News.
And that concern is somewhat warranted, he said, especially after the bank didn't raise rates quickly in the face of high inflation post-COVID. The signal today is that the bank doesn't want a redo of that.
"I think the bank is concerned about this oil price shock playing a role here in the same way that it did in 2022. And you know, who can blame them? They're a little nervous about how that might play out."
Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel
Crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are slowly recovering, so why is the price of diesel skyrocketing? The National's Eli Glasner breaks down what’s causing the increase, and why diesel prices likely won't drop anytime soon.
Rising oil prices linked to war in the Middle East have been a persistent irritant for the Bank of Canada as it attempts to control inflation. That war could escalate in the coming weeks.
U.S. officials have told several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday .
The U.S. benchmark oil price soared nearly 3.5 per cent today, rising above $103 US per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude is up nearly 70 per cent year-over-year.
According to data from Kalibrate, Canadian pump prices for regular gasoline are up nearly 30 per cent on average versus this time last year. Diesel prices have soared over 70 per cent on an annualized basis.
Here's what the Bank of Canada said about the situation earlier today:
"The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month, and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices, and increased pass-through, adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection.
"The prices of gasoline, diesel and heating oil are considerably higher than in July, and are expected to remain higher for longer. This is hitting consumers directly and raising business costs for production and transportation."
Benjamin Reitzes, managing director at BMO Economics, says the central bank's messaging indicates further hikes will come — but maybe not soon.
Despite the Bank of Canada warning that more rate hikes might be necessary, it also said it would proceed with caution. That "suggests a follow-up hike in December isn't a lock by any means," Reitzes said.
"There's likely more tightening to come, but the pace of further hikes is extremely uncertain and will be driven by the incoming data," he wrote in a note to investors.
Reitzes says weak growth forecasted for the last few months of this year and continued trade uncertainty will be the things to watch — and that if momentum picks up there, that could trigger more increases.
Heading into today's decision, business owners across Canada were already in a tough spot.
The trade war with the U.S. has been a significant weight and increased the cost of doing business, according to Simon Gaudreault, chief economist for the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB).
"We're talking about entrepreneurs that have been entrepreneurs for 15, 20, 25 years or more, telling us that they've never seen such a challenging situation in terms of the operating costs," Gaudreault said.
Today's rate hike could add to that pain for lots of businesses, he said. A rate hike would leave Canadian consumers with less cash in their pockets, which Gauldreaut says could hurt demand for business owners.
Many business owners also have variable mortgages for business properties or hold other kinds of debt at floating rates, he said, meaning their costs will now be higher. It could also make it harder to take on new business investments, like upgrading equipment.
"The trade war hasn't brought that sort of certainty that you're looking for as an entrepreneur to invest. And so making the cost of capital even higher, even more expensive with the rate hike certainly won't help here."
